claim: EMA2 mRNA is exclusively expressed during conjugation
source: EMA2 mRNA is exclusively expressed during conjugation (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 1A, which displays expression levels across different cell states.

claim: Ema2 protein first appeared in the MAC during conjugation at 3 hr post-induction of mating (hpm) and 6 hpm
source: The encoded Ema2 protein tagged with HA at the endogenous EMA2 locus was not detectable in the vegetative cells (Figure 1B, Vg) and first appeared in the MAC during conjugation (Figure 1B, 3 hr post-induction of mating [hpm] and 6 hpm).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At the onset of new MAC development, Ema2 disappeared from the parental MAC and appeared in the new MAC
source: At the onset of new MAC development, Ema2 disappeared from the parental MAC and appeared in the new MAC (Figure 1B, 8 hpm), which later faded away (Figures 1B, 12, and 14 hpm).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B at different time points.

claim: The conjugation-specific expression and the localization switch from the parental to the new MAC are reminiscent of the factors involved in DNA elimination such as the Piwi protein Twi1 and PRC2
source: The conjugation-specific expression and the localization switch from the parental to the new MAC are reminiscent of the factors involved in DNA elimination such as the Piwi protein Twi1, which is loaded by scnRNAs, and PRC2 (Liu et al., 2007; Mochizuki et al., 2002; Noto et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to previously published findings about Twi1 and PRC2.

claim: DNA elimination is completed by ~14–18 hpm in wild-type cells
source: DNA elimination is completed by ~14–18 hpm in wild-type cells (Austerberry et al., 1984; Mutazono et al., 2019), and the Tlr1 element was detected only in the MICs in the exconjugants from wild-type cells (Figure 2A, WT).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by FISH data in Figure 2A.

claim: The Tlr1 element was detected in both the MICs and the MACs in the exconjugants from the EMA2 somatic KO strains
source: In contrast, the Tlr1 element was detected in both the MICs and the MACs in the exconjugants from the EMA2 somatic KO strains, in which all EMA2 copies in the MAC were disrupted (Shehzada and Mochizuki, 2022; Figure 2A, KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The intensity of the FISH signal in the new MACs was lower in the exconjugants from the EMA2 KO cells than in those from the TWI1 KO cells
source: The intensity of the FISH signal in the new MACs was lower in the exconjugants from the EMA2 KO cells than in those from the TWI1 KO cells (Figure 2B), in the latter of which DNA elimination is known to be completely blocked (Noto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative FISH data shown in Figure 2B and comparison to TWI1 KO cells.

claim: DNA elimination was partially blocked in the exconjugants of EMA2 KO cells
source: Therefore, DNA elimination was partially blocked in the exconjugants of EMA2 KO cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the FISH signal intensity data comparing EMA2 KO to wild-type and TWI1 KO cells.

claim: EMA2 KO cells did not produce viable progeny
source: Consistent with the requirement of DNA elimination in the viability of sexual progeny (Cheng et al., 2010; Vogt and Mochizuki, 2013), EMA2 KO cells did not produce viable progeny (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability test data shown in Figure 2C and citations to previous studies.

claim: Maternally expressed EMA2 is required for completing DNA elimination
source: Altogether, we conclude that maternally expressed EMA2 is required for completing DNA elimination.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the DNA elimination and viability data.

claim: The production of scnRNAs occurs from IESs and their surrounding MDS regions in the MIC at the early conjugation stages (~2–3 hpm)
source: The production of scnRNAs occurs from IESs and their surrounding MDS regions in the MIC at the early conjugation stages (~2–3 hpm), and scnRNAs complementary to the MAC genome (=MDSs) are subjected to TDSD in the parental MAC in the mid-conjugation stages (~3–7 hpm), resulting in the selective retention of IES-derived scnRNAs that later target IESs for DNA elimination in the new MAC (Aronica et al., 2008; Mochizuki and Gorovsky, 2004b; Noto et al., 2015; Schoeberl et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: scnRNAs complementary to the MAC genome are subjected to TDSD in the parental MAC in the mid-conjugation stages (~3–7 hpm)
source: The production of scnRNAs occurs from IESs and their surrounding MDS regions in the MIC at the early conjugation stages (~2–3 hpm), and scnRNAs complementary to the MAC genome (=MDSs) are subjected to TDSD in the parental MAC in the mid-conjugation stages (~3–7 hpm), resulting in the selective retention of IES-derived scnRNAs that later target IESs for DNA elimination in the new MAC (Aronica et al., 2008; Mochizuki and Gorovsky, 2004b; Noto et al., 2015; Schoeberl et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In wild-type cells, the Mi-9-complementary scnRNAs were detected at 3 hpm, reduced at 4.5 hpm, and became undetectable at 6 hpm due to TDSD
source: Because scnRNAs detected by this probe are complementary to the MAC genome, in wild-type cells, the Mi-9-complementary scnRNAs were detected at 3 hpm, reduced at 4.5 hpm, and became undetectable at 6 hpm due to TDSD (Figure 3A, WT).
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Mi-9-complementary scnRNAs remained detectable at 6 hpm in the EMA2 KO cells
source: In contrast, the Mi-9-complementary scnRNAs remained detectable at 6 hpm in the EMA2 KO cells (Figure 3A, KO), suggesting that Ema2 is required for TDSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by northern blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ema2 is required for TDSD
source: In contrast, the Mi-9-complementary scnRNAs remained detectable at 6 hpm in the EMA2 KO cells (Figure 3A, KO), suggesting that Ema2 is required for TDSD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the northern blot data showing persistence of scnRNAs in EMA2 KO cells.

claim: scnRNAs that mapped many of the MDS tiles were greatly reduced from 3 to 8 hpm due to TDSD in the wild-type cells
source: Although scnRNAs that mapped many of the MDS tiles were greatly reduced from 3 to 8 hpm due to TDSD in the wild-type cells (Figure 3B, left, WT), those in the EMA2 KO cells were only slightly reduced by 8 hpm (Figure 3B, left, EMA2 KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: scnRNAs in the EMA2 KO cells were only slightly reduced by 8 hpm
source: Although scnRNAs that mapped many of the MDS tiles were greatly reduced from 3 to 8 hpm due to TDSD in the wild-type cells (Figure 3B, left, WT), those in the EMA2 KO cells were only slightly reduced by 8 hpm (Figure 3B, left, EMA2 KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The increased abundance of MDS-complementary scnRNAs at 3 hpm in the EMA2 KO cells compared to the wild-type cells can be attributed to the necessity of Ema2 in TDSD
source: Because TDSD takes place concurrently with the scnRNA production (Schoeberl et al., 2012), the increased abundance of MDS-complementary scnRNAs at 3 hpm in the EMA2 KO cells compared to the wild-type cells can also be attributed to the necessity of Ema2 in TDSD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the small RNA sequencing data and previous knowledge about TDSD timing.

claim: The TDSD defect in the EMA2 KO cells seems milder than that in the EMA1 KO cells
source: This TDSD defect in the EMA2 KO cells seems milder than that in the EMA1 KO cells, in which the amount of MDS-complementary scnRNAs remained constant until 8 hpm (Figure 3B, left, EMA1 KO), indicating that Ema1 and Ema2 act differently in TDSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of small RNA sequencing data between EMA2 KO and EMA1 KO cells shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Ema1 and Ema2 act differently in TDSD
source: This TDSD defect in the EMA2 KO cells seems milder than that in the EMA1 KO cells, in which the amount of MDS-complementary scnRNAs remained constant until 8 hpm (Figure 3B, left, EMA1 KO), indicating that Ema1 and Ema2 act differently in TDSD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of TDSD defects between EMA2 KO and EMA1 KO cells.

claim: The amounts of scnRNAs complementary to IES tiles at 3 hpm and 8 hpm were comparable in all strains
source: In contrast, the amounts of scnRNAs complementary to IES tiles at 3 hpm and 8 hpm were comparable in all strains (Figure 3B, right), which is consistent with previous observations that only scnRNAs complementary to MDSs are targeted for TDSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by small RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only scnRNAs complementary to MDSs are targeted for TDSD
source: In contrast, the amounts of scnRNAs complementary to IES tiles at 3 hpm and 8 hpm were comparable in all strains (Figure 3B, right), which is consistent with previous observations that only scnRNAs complementary to MDSs are targeted for TDSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by the current data and previous observations.

claim: Ema2 is required for TDSD at the genome-wide level
source: These results suggest that Ema2 is required for TDSD at the genome-wide level.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the small RNA sequencing data across multiple genomic tiles.

claim: Loss of TDSD results in a partial block of DNA elimination
source: Because it is known that loss of TDSD results in a partial block of DNA elimination (Aronica et al., 2008), the mild DNA elimination defect in EMA2 KO cells (Figure 2B) can be explained by the requirement of Ema2 in TDSD.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The mild DNA elimination defect in EMA2 KO cells can be explained by the requirement of Ema2 in TDSD
source: Because it is known that loss of TDSD results in a partial block of DNA elimination (Aronica et al., 2008), the mild DNA elimination defect in EMA2 KO cells (Figure 2B) can be explained by the requirement of Ema2 in TDSD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the connection between TDSD defect and DNA elimination defect.

claim: Ema2 possesses an SP-RING domain that has been found in many SUMO E3 ligases
source: Ema2 possesses an SP-RING domain that has been found in many SUMO E3 ligases (Hochstrasser, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous work and domain analysis.

claim: The SP-RING domain of Ema2 is atypical in that the first cysteine of the zinc ion-binding residues in typical counterparts is replaced by histidine
source: The SP-RING domain of Ema2 is atypical (Figure 4A) in that the first cysteine of the zinc ion-binding residues in typical counterparts is replaced by histidine and some of the stabilizer residues (Duan et al., 2009; Yunus and Lima, 2009) are likely missing.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Some of the stabilizer residues in the SP-RING domain of Ema2 are likely missing
source: The SP-RING domain of Ema2 is atypical (Figure 4A) in that the first cysteine of the zinc ion-binding residues in typical counterparts is replaced by histidine and some of the stabilizer residues (Duan et al., 2009; Yunus and Lima, 2009) are likely missing.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Ema2 can directly interact with the Tetrahymena SUMO E2 enzyme Ubc9 in vitro
source: We indeed found that Ema2 can directly interact with the Tetrahymena SUMO E2 enzyme Ubc9 in vitro (Figure 4B), suggesting that Ema2 is a bona fide SUMO E3 ligase.
evidence: The claim is supported by GST pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ema2 is a bona fide SUMO E3 ligase
source: We indeed found that Ema2 can directly interact with the Tetrahymena SUMO E2 enzyme Ubc9 in vitro (Figure 4B), suggesting that Ema2 is a bona fide SUMO E3 ligase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the interaction with Ubc9 and the presence of an SP-RING domain.

claim: High molecular weight proteins (mainly >200 kDa) were detected in the WT cross at 4.5 and 6 hpm
source: At both time points, high molecular weight proteins (mainly >200 kDa) were detected in the WT cross (Figure 4C, WT), and they were reduced to ~50% in the EMA2 KO cross (Figure 4C, KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: High molecular weight SUMOylated proteins were reduced to ~50% in the EMA2 KO cross
source: At both time points, high molecular weight proteins (mainly >200 kDa) were detected in the WT cross (Figure 4C, WT), and they were reduced to ~50% in the EMA2 KO cross (Figure 4C, KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Ema2 is the major SUMO E3 ligase during the mid-conjugation stages
source: These results indicate that Ema2 is the major SUMO E3 ligase during the mid-conjugation stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the substantial reduction in SUMOylated proteins in EMA2 KO cells.

claim: The remaining Ema2-independent SUMOylation is likely mediated by other SUMO E3 ligases and/or E3-independent SUMOylation
source: The remaining Ema2-independent SUMOylation is likely mediated by other SUMO E3 ligases (including the SP-RING containing proteins TTHERM_00227730, TTHERM_00442270 and TTHERM_00348490), and/or E3-independent SUMOylation (Sampson et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the presence of residual SUMOylation in EMA2 KO cells and knowledge of other potential SUMO E3 ligases.

claim: The requirement of protein SUMOylation in DNA elimination was previously demonstrated in Paramecium by RNAi knockdown of UBA2 and SUMO
source: The requirement of protein SUMOylation in DNA elimination was previously demonstrated in Paramecium by RNAi knockdown of UBA2, the gene encoding the SUMO E1 enzyme, and SUMO (Matsuda and Forney, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The involvement of a SUMO pathway in DNA elimination is likely conserved among ciliates
source: Therefore, the involvement of a SUMO pathway in DNA elimination is likely conserved among ciliates.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the requirement of SUMOylation in both Tetrahymena and Paramecium.

claim: Spt6 was the most abundantly detected protein in the WT cross
source: Although most of the proteins were detected similarly between the WT cross and EMA2 KO cross, Spt6, the most abundantly detected protein in the WT cross, was detected at a much lower level in the EMA2 KO cross (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Spt6 was detected at a much lower level in the EMA2 KO cross compared to the WT cross
source: Although most of the proteins were detected similarly between the WT cross and EMA2 KO cross, Spt6, the most abundantly detected protein in the WT cross, was detected at a much lower level in the EMA2 KO cross (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Spt6 is the major Ema2 target for SUMOylation
source: This result suggests that Spt6 is the major Ema2 target for SUMOylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mass spectrometry data showing reduced Spt6 detection in EMA2 KO cells.

claim: A slower migrating population of Spt6-HA was detected in addition to a band corresponding to unmodified Spt6-HA at 4.5 and 6 hpm in the WT cross
source: In the WT cross, a slower migrating population of Spt6-HA was detected in addition to a band corresponding to unmodified Spt6-HA at both time points (Figure 5B, WT).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Slower migrating Spt6-HA was barely detectable in the EMA2 KO cross
source: In contrast, slower migrating Spt6-HA was barely detectable in the EMA2 KO cross (Figure 5B, KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The slower migrating species of Spt6-HA were not detected in growing and starved vegetative wild-type cells when Ema2 was not expressed
source: Consistent with the Ema2-dependent appearance of the slower migrating Spt6-HA, they were not detected in growing and starved vegetative wild-type cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Veg and 0 hpm, respectively) when Ema2 was not expressed (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and the expression pattern of Ema2 shown in Figure 1.

claim: The slower migrating Spt6-HA was detected at 8 hpm when the new MAC was already formed
source: The slower migrating Spt6-HA was also detected at 8 hpm when the new MAC was already formed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, 8 hpm) suggesting that Spt6 is possibly SUMOylated also in the new MAC.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spt6 is possibly SUMOylated also in the new MAC
source: The slower migrating Spt6-HA was also detected at 8 hpm when the new MAC was already formed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, 8 hpm) suggesting that Spt6 is possibly SUMOylated also in the new MAC.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the detection of slower migrating Spt6-HA at 8 hpm.

claim: The slower migrating species of Spt6-HA were detected by an anti-Smt3 antibody in the WT cross
source: Among the total purified Spt6-HA (Figure 5C, left, IP-WT), the slower migrating species were detected by an anti-Smt3 antibody in the WT cross (Figure 5C, right, IP-WT), and such SUMOylated Spt6-HA species were greatly reduced in the EMA2 KO cross (Figure 5C, KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SUMOylated Spt6-HA species were greatly reduced in the EMA2 KO cross
source: Among the total purified Spt6-HA (Figure 5C, left, IP-WT), the slower migrating species were detected by an anti-Smt3 antibody in the WT cross (Figure 5C, right, IP-WT), and such SUMOylated Spt6-HA species were greatly reduced in the EMA2 KO cross (Figure 5C, KO).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The slower migrating species of Spt6 are SUMOylated Spt6
source: These results indicate that the slower migrating species of Spt6 are SUMOylated Spt6 and Ema2 is required for the majority of SUMOylation of Spt6 during the mid-conjugation stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the detection of slower migrating Spt6 by anti-Smt3 antibody.

claim: Ema2 is required for the majority of SUMOylation of Spt6 during the mid-conjugation stages
source: These results indicate that the slower migrating species of Spt6 are SUMOylated Spt6 and Ema2 is required for the majority of SUMOylation of Spt6 during the mid-conjugation stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the reduction of SUMOylated Spt6 in EMA2 KO cells.

claim: The remaining SUMOylation observed on Spt6 in the absence of Ema2 is likely facilitated by other SUMO E3 ligases and/or E3-independent SUMOylation
source: The remaining SUMOylation observed on Spt6 in the absence of Ema2 is likely facilitated by other SUMO E3 ligases and/or E3-independent SUMOylation, as discussed earlier for the other instances of Ema2-independent SUMOylations.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the presence of residual Spt6 SUMOylation in EMA2 KO cells.

claim: Spt6 is a conserved regulator of several steps of transcription in various eukaryotes
source: Spt6 is a conserved regulator of several steps of transcription in various eukaryotes.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about Spt6.

claim: TDSD was proposed to be triggered by the base-pairing interaction between scnRNAs and nascent pMAC-lncRNAs in the parental MAC
source: Because TDSD was proposed to be triggered by the base-pairing interaction between scnRNAs and nascent pMAC-lncRNAs in the parental MAC (Aronica et al., 2008; Noto and Mochizuki, 2018), we hypothesized that Ema2-dependent Spt6 SUMOylation promotes pMAC-lncRNA transcription.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ema2-dependent Spt6 SUMOylation promotes pMAC-lncRNA transcription
source: Because TDSD was proposed to be triggered by the base-pairing interaction between scnRNAs and nascent pMAC-lncRNAs in the parental MAC (Aronica et al., 2008; Noto and Mochizuki, 2018), we hypothesized that Ema2-dependent Spt6 SUMOylation promotes pMAC-lncRNA transcription.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the role of Spt6 in transcription and the requirement of pMAC-lncRNAs for TDSD.

claim: pMAC-lncRNAs were detected in wild-type cells but not in EMA2 KO cells at 6 hpm for three tested loci
source: For the three loci examined, pMAC-lncRNAs were detected in wild-type cells but not in EMA2 KO cells at 6 hpm, although the control RPL21 mRNA was detected in both conditions (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The lack of detection of pMAC-lncRNAs in EMA2 KO cells was not due to loss of the primer binding sites by alternative DNA elimination
source: The lack of detection of pMAC-lncRNAs in EMA2 KO cells was not due to loss of the primer binding sites by alternative DNA elimination in their prior sexual reproductions, as genomic PCR with the same primer sets detected the corresponding MAC loci in the EMA2 KO cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ema2 is required for the accumulation of pMAC-lncRNAs at least for the three tested loci
source: We, therefore, conclude that Ema2 is required for the accumulation of pMAC-lncRNAs at least for the three tested loci.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the RT-PCR data.

claim: Long dsRNAs were detected first in the MIC at 3 hpm, then in the parental MAC at 6 hpm, and finally in the new MAC at 9 hpm in wild-type cells
source: As previously reported, immunostaining of wild-type cells using the long double-stranded (ds)RNA-specific J2 antibody (Schönborn et al., 1991; Figure 6B, WT) detected long dsRNAs first in the MIC at its premeiotic stage (3 hpm), then in the parental MAC at the mid stages of conjugation (6 hpm), and finally in the new MAC at late conjugation (9 hpm).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Long dsRNAs were detected in the MIC at 3 hpm and in the new MAC at 9 hpm but were undetectable in the parental MAC at 6 hpm in the EMA2 KO cells
source: In the EMA2 KO cells, long dsRNAs were detected in the MIC at 3 hpm and in the new MAC at 9 hpm but were undetectable in the parental MAC at 6 hpm (Figure 6B, EMA2 KO), indicating that Ema2 is specifically required for the accumulation of pMAC-lncRNAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Ema2 is specifically required for the accumulation of pMAC-lncRNAs
source: In the EMA2 KO cells, long dsRNAs were detected in the MIC at 3 hpm and in the new MAC at 9 hpm but were undetectable in the parental MAC at 6 hpm (Figure 6B, EMA2 KO), indicating that Ema2 is specifically required for the accumulation of pMAC-lncRNAs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the specific loss of dsRNA signal in the parental MAC in EMA2 KO cells.

claim: EMA1 was dispensable for the accumulation of dsRNAs in the parental MAC
source: In contrast, EMA1 was dispensable for the accumulation of dsRNAs in the parental MAC (Figure 6B, EMA1 KO), which is consistent with the previous notions that Ema1 is required for pMAC-lncRNAs to interact with scnRNAs but not their transcription (Aronica et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Ema1 is required for pMAC-lncRNAs to interact with scnRNAs but not their transcription
source: In contrast, EMA1 was dispensable for the accumulation of dsRNAs in the parental MAC (Figure 6B, EMA1 KO), which is consistent with the previous notions that Ema1 is required for pMAC-lncRNAs to interact with scnRNAs but not their transcription (Aronica et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The less severe TDSD defect observed in the EMA2 KO cells compared to the EMA1 KO cells indicates that certain Ema1-dependent TDSD may be initiated by single-stranded lncRNAs or mRNAs that are transcribed independently of Ema2
source: Although it is unclear whether lncRNAs are single or double-stranded when Ema1 promotes the lncRNA-scnRNAs interaction, the less severe TDSD defect observed in the EMA2 KO cells compared to the EMA1 KO cells (Figure 3B) indicates that certain Ema1-dependent TDSD may be initiated by single-stranded lncRNAs or mRNAs that are transcribed independently of Ema2.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the comparison of TDSD defects between EMA2 KO and EMA1 KO cells.

claim: scnRNA-dependent accumulation of H3K27me3 occurs in the parental MAC
source: In parallel to TDSD, scnRNA-dependent accumulation of H3K27me3, which is catalyzed by the histone methyltransferase Ezl1 within PRC2, occurs in the parental MAC (Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: H3K27me3 was undetectable in the parental MAC in the EMA2 KO cells at 6 hpm
source: We found that H3K27me3 was undetectable in the parental MAC in the EMA2 KO cells at 6 hpm or in the EMA1, TWI1, and EZL1 KO cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: H3K27me3 was undetectable in the parental MAC in the EMA1, TWI1, and EZL1 KO cells
source: We found that H3K27me3 was undetectable in the parental MAC in the EMA2 KO cells at 6 hpm or in the EMA1, TWI1, and EZL1 KO cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Ema2 is required for the scnRNA-directed deposition of H3K27me3 in the parental MAC
source: Therefore, Ema2 is required for the scnRNA-directed deposition of H3K27me3 in the parental MAC, which can be explained by the loss of the chromatin recruitment of PRC2 by the scnRNA-lncRNA interaction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss of H3K27me3 in EMA2 KO cells.

claim: The loss of H3K27me3 in EMA2 KO cells can be explained by the loss of the chromatin recruitment of PRC2 by the scnRNA-lncRNA interaction
source: Therefore, Ema2 is required for the scnRNA-directed deposition of H3K27me3 in the parental MAC, which can be explained by the loss of the chromatin recruitment of PRC2 by the scnRNA-lncRNA interaction.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the requirement of lncRNAs for scnRNA-directed chromatin modifications.

claim: Ema2 is required for the genome-wide accumulation of pMAC-lncRNAs
source: Altogether, these results indicate that Ema2 is required for the genome-wide accumulation of pMAC-lncRNAs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the RT-PCR, immunofluorescence, and H3K27me3 data.

claim: Spt6-HA was similarly detected in the MAC at 4.5 hpm in both WT and EMA2 KO cross
source: In both WT and EMA2 KO cross described above, Spt6-HA was similarly detected in the MAC at 4.5 hpm (Figure 7A, left) and in the new MAC at 9 hpm (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Spt6-HA was similarly detected in the new MAC at 9 hpm in both WT and EMA2 KO cross
source: In both WT and EMA2 KO cross described above, Spt6-HA was similarly detected in the MAC at 4.5 hpm (Figure 7A, left) and in the new MAC at 9 hpm (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MAC localization of Rpb3 was not affected in the absence of Ema2
source: We also found that the MAC localization of Rpb3, the third largest subunit of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) was not affected in the absence of Ema2 (Figure 7A, right).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: At the cytological level, the absence of Ema2 does not affect the localization of Spt6 and RNAPII
source: Therefore, at least at the cytological level, the absence of Ema2 does not affect the localization of Spt6 and RNAPII.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the immunofluorescence data.

claim: In the WT cross, Spt6-HA was detected in both the soluble (S1) and chromatin-bound (S2) fractions
source: In the WT cross (Figure 7B, WT), Spt6-HA was detected in both the soluble (S1) and chromatin-bound (S2) fractions, but slower-migrating SUMOylated Spt6-HA was detected only in the latter fraction, indicating that SUMOylated Spt6 is associated with chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Slower-migrating SUMOylated Spt6-HA was detected only in the chromatin-bound fraction
source: In the WT cross (Figure 7B, WT), Spt6-HA was detected in both the soluble (S1) and chromatin-bound (S2) fractions, but slower-migrating SUMOylated Spt6-HA was detected only in the latter fraction, indicating that SUMOylated Spt6 is associated with chromatin.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SUMOylated Spt6 is associated with chromatin
source: In the WT cross (Figure 7B, WT), Spt6-HA was detected in both the soluble (S1) and chromatin-bound (S2) fractions, but slower-migrating SUMOylated Spt6-HA was detected only in the latter fraction, indicating that SUMOylated Spt6 is associated with chromatin.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the detection of SUMOylated Spt6 only in the chromatin-bound fraction.

claim: Rpb3 showed a similar distribution to Spt6-HA in the cell fractionation assay
source: A similar distribution was detected for Rpb3.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The chromatin association of Spt6 and RNAPII does not require RNA
source: This chromatin association of Spt6 and RNAPII does not require RNA, as they were retained in the insoluble fraction after RNase A treatment without sonication (Figure 7C), although Twi1, which interacts with chromatin through nascent pMAC-lncRNA (Aronica et al., 2008), was mostly detected in the soluble fraction after the treatment (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation with RNase treatment data shown in Figure 7C and citation to a previous study.

claim: Twi1 interacts with chromatin through nascent pMAC-lncRNA
source: This chromatin association of Spt6 and RNAPII does not require RNA, as they were retained in the insoluble fraction after RNase A treatment without sonication (Figure 7C), although Twi1, which interacts with chromatin through nascent pMAC-lncRNA (Aronica et al., 2008), was mostly detected in the soluble fraction after the treatment (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the EMA2 KO cross, Spt6-HA and Rpb3 in the chromatin-bound fraction were greatly reduced
source: In the EMA2 KO cross, Spt6-HA and Rpb3 in the chromatin-bound fraction were greatly reduced (Figure 7B, KO, S2).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation and western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Ema2 promotes the association of Spt6 and RNAPII with chromatin in the parental MAC at the mid-conjugation stage
source: We, therefore, conclude that Ema2 promotes the association of Spt6 and RNAPII with chromatin in the parental MAC at the mid-conjugation stage.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the cell fractionation data.

claim: HA-Smt3 could replace the essential function of endogenous Smt3
source: SUMO is solely encoded by SMT3 in Tetrahymena (Nasir et al., 2015), and HA-Smt3 could replace the essential function of endogenous Smt3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation to a previous study.

claim: SUMO is solely encoded by SMT3 in Tetrahymena
source: SUMO is solely encoded by SMT3 in Tetrahymena (Nasir et al., 2015), and HA-Smt3 could replace the essential function of endogenous Smt3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: All SPT6 mutant constructs were able to restore the lethality of SPT6 KO cells
source: We introduced these mutant constructs as well as the construct expressing wild-type Spt6 (HA-SPT6-WT) into SPT6 KO cells and found that all of them were able to restore the lethality of SPT6 KO cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The cells rescued by HA-SPT6-N-KR showed severe defects in meiotic progression
source: However, the cells rescued by HA-SPT6-N-KR and HA-SPT6-M-KR showed severe defects in meiotic progression and mating initiation, respectively, making their SUMOylation status during conjugation uninvestigable.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during the experiments.

claim: The cells rescued by HA-SPT6-M-KR showed severe defects in mating initiation
source: However, the cells rescued by HA-SPT6-N-KR and HA-SPT6-M-KR showed severe defects in meiotic progression and mating initiation, respectively, making their SUMOylation status during conjugation uninvestigable.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during the experiments.

claim: The cells rescued by HA-SPT6-DOL-KR and HA-SPT6-C-KR showed a seemingly normal progression of conjugation
source: In contrast, the cells rescued by HA-SPT6-DOL-KR and HA-SPT6-C-KR showed a seemingly normal progression of conjugation, although the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells showed lower mating efficiency.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during the experiments.

claim: The HA-SPT6-C-KR cells showed lower mating efficiency
source: In contrast, the cells rescued by HA-SPT6-DOL-KR and HA-SPT6-C-KR showed a seemingly normal progression of conjugation, although the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells showed lower mating efficiency.
evidence: The claim is based on observations during the experiments.

claim: HA-Spt6-DOL-KR was SUMOylated like HA-Spt6-WT
source: We found that while HA-Spt6-DOL-KR was SUMOylated like HA-Spt6-WT, SUMOylation was not detected on HA-Spt6-C-KR (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: SUMOylation was not detected on HA-Spt6-C-KR
source: We found that while HA-Spt6-DOL-KR was SUMOylated like HA-Spt6-WT, SUMOylation was not detected on HA-Spt6-C-KR (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Spt6-C-KR represents a SUMOylation-defective Spt6 mutant
source: Therefore, Spt6-C-KR represents a SUMOylation-defective Spt6 mutant, exhibiting at least a reduced level of SUMOylation compared to Spt6 in the absence of Ema2 (compare Figure 8B and Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the western blot data comparing Spt6-C-KR to wild-type and EMA2 KO conditions.

claim: HA-Spt6 and RNAPII were detected in the chromatin-bound fraction in HA-SPT6-C-KR cells as in the HA-SPT6-WT cells
source: Cell fractionation experiments showed that HA-Spt6 and RNAPII were detected in the chromatin-bound fraction in HA-SPT6-C-KR cells as in the HA-SPT6-WT cells consistently in three independent experiments (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 2), and long dsRNAs were detected in the parental MAC (Figure 8D) as well as in the new MAC (Figure 8—figure supplement 3) in the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell fractionation data shown in Figure 8C and Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: Long dsRNAs were detected in the parental MAC in the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells
source: Cell fractionation experiments showed that HA-Spt6 and RNAPII were detected in the chromatin-bound fraction in HA-SPT6-C-KR cells as in the HA-SPT6-WT cells consistently in three independent experiments (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 2), and long dsRNAs were detected in the parental MAC (Figure 8D) as well as in the new MAC (Figure 8—figure supplement 3) in the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Long dsRNAs were detected in the new MAC in the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells
source: Cell fractionation experiments showed that HA-Spt6 and RNAPII were detected in the chromatin-bound fraction in HA-SPT6-C-KR cells as in the HA-SPT6-WT cells consistently in three independent experiments (Figure 8C, Figure 8—figure supplement 2), and long dsRNAs were detected in the parental MAC (Figure 8D) as well as in the new MAC (Figure 8—figure supplement 3) in the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claim: Spt6 SUMOylation per se is not required for the lncRNA transcription in the parental MAC
source: These results suggest that, contrary to our expectation, Spt6 SUMOylation per se is not required for the lncRNA transcription in the parental MAC.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the observation that the SUMOylation-defective Spt6-C-KR mutant still supports lncRNA transcription.

claim: Exconjugants from the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells showed a mild DNA elimination defect
source: Nonetheless, exconjugants from the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells showed a mild DNA elimination defect (Figure 8E), indicating that Ema2-directed Spt6-SUMOylation plays a role in DNA elimination other than promoting pMAC-lncRNA transcription.
evidence: The claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Ema2-directed Spt6-SUMOylation plays a role in DNA elimination other than promoting pMAC-lncRNA transcription
source: Nonetheless, exconjugants from the HA-SPT6-C-KR cells showed a mild DNA elimination defect (Figure 8E), indicating that Ema2-directed Spt6-SUMOylation plays a role in DNA elimination other than promoting pMAC-lncRNA transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the DNA elimination defect in Spt6-C-KR cells despite normal lncRNA transcription.

claim: The conjugation-specific SUMO E3 ligase Ema2 is required for the accumulation of lncRNAs in the parental MAC
source: In this study, we showed that the conjugation-specific SUMO E3 ligase Ema2 is required for the accumulation of lncRNAs (Figure 6), TDSD (Figure 3A and B), and heterochromatin formation (Figure 3C) in the parental MAC and eventually for completing DNA elimination (Figure 1) in Tetrahymena.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by multiple figures.

claim: Ema2 is required for TDSD in the parental MAC
source: In this study, we showed that the conjugation-specific SUMO E3 ligase Ema2 is required for the accumulation of lncRNAs (Figure 6), TDSD (Figure 3A and B), and heterochromatin formation (Figure 3C) in the parental MAC and eventually for completing DNA elimination (Figure 1) in Tetrahymena.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by multiple figures.

claim: Ema2 is required for heterochromatin formation in the parental MAC
source: In this study, we showed that the conjugation-specific SUMO E3 ligase Ema2 is required for the accumulation of lncRNAs (Figure 6), TDSD (Figure 3A and B), and heterochromatin formation (Figure 3C) in the parental MAC and eventually for completing DNA elimination (Figure 1) in Tetrahymena.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by multiple figures.

claim: Ema2 is responsible for SUMOylation of the transcription regulator Spt6
source: We found that Ema2 is responsible for SUMOylation of the transcriptional regulator Spt6 (Figure 5) and promotes the interaction of Spt6 and RNAPII with chromatin (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by multiple figures.

claim: Ema2 promotes the interaction of Spt6 and RNAPII with chromatin
source: We found that Ema2 is responsible for SUMOylation of the transcriptional regulator Spt6 (Figure 5) and promotes the interaction of Spt6 and RNAPII with chromatin (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main findings supported by multiple figures.

claim: Ema2 facilitates genome-wide lncRNA transcription in the parental MAC
source: We, therefore, conclude that Ema2 facilitates genome-wide lncRNA transcription in the parental MAC, which is a prerequisite for scnRNA-chromatin communication and thus for the downstream TDSD that regulates DNA elimination.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the collective findings of the study.

claim: lncRNA transcription in the parental MAC is a prerequisite for scnRNA-chromatin communication
source: We, therefore, conclude that Ema2 facilitates genome-wide lncRNA transcription in the parental MAC, which is a prerequisite for scnRNA-chromatin communication and thus for the downstream TDSD that regulates DNA elimination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the requirement of lncRNAs for TDSD and heterochromatin formation.

claim: The observed loss of the majority of Spt6 and RNAPII from chromatin in the absence of Ema2 must be a temporal event during the mid-conjugation stage
source: Therefore, the observed loss of the majority of Spt6 and RNAPII from chromatin in the absence of Ema2 (Figure 7B) must be a temporal event during the mid-conjugation stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the fact that Spt6 and RNAPII are essential for vegetative growth and conjugation progression.

claim: Spt6 and RNAPII might be specifically engaged in pMAC-lncRNA transcription at the mid-conjugation stage in wild-type cells
source: This suggests that Spt6 and RNAPII might be specifically engaged in pMAC-lncRNA transcription at this particular time window in wild-type cells.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the temporal loss of Spt6 and RNAPII from chromatin in EMA2 KO cells.

claim: Some radical change in the chromatin environment in the parental MAC is required for the global transcription of pMAC-lncRNAs
source: It is likely that some radical change in the chromatin environment in the parental MAC is required for the global transcription of pMAC-lncRNAs, and Ema2-dependent SUMOylation might maintain Spt6 and RNAPII on chromatin for transcription in such an environment.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for the role of Ema2.

claim: Ema2-dependent SUMOylation might maintain Spt6 and RNAPII on chromatin for transcription in a changed chromatin environment
source: It is likely that some radical change in the chromatin environment in the parental MAC is required for the global transcription of pMAC-lncRNAs, and Ema2-dependent SUMOylation might maintain Spt6 and RNAPII on chromatin for transcription in such an environment.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for the role of Ema2.

claim: The transcription of pMAC-lncRNAs might require a greater amount of transcriptional machinery than other types of transcription
source: Alternatively, because the expression of many of the transcriptional machineries, including Spt6 and RNAPII subunits, is highly upregulated during conjugation (Miao et al., 2009; Mochizuki and Gorovsky, 2004a; Xiong et al., 2012), the transcription of pMAC-lncRNAs might require a greater amount of transcriptional machinery than other types of transcription, and Ema2-dependent SUMOylation might be required for committing these excess machineries to chromatin for transcription.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as an alternative explanation for the role of Ema2, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ema2-dependent SUMOylation might be required for committing excess transcriptional machineries to chromatin for transcription
source: Alternatively, because the expression of many of the transcriptional machineries, including Spt6 and RNAPII subunits, is highly upregulated during conjugation (Miao et al., 2009; Mochizuki and Gorovsky, 2004a; Xiong et al., 2012), the transcription of pMAC-lncRNAs might require a greater amount of transcriptional machinery than other types of transcription, and Ema2-dependent SUMOylation might be required for committing these excess machineries to chromatin for transcription.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as an alternative explanation for the role of Ema2.

claim: Ema2 may facilitate pMAC-lncRNA transcription through SUMOylation of some protein(s) other than Spt6
source: This observation suggests that Ema2 may facilitate pMAC-lncRNA transcription through SUMOylation of some protein(s) other than Spt6.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that SUMOylation-defective Spt6 still supports lncRNA transcription.

claim: Some Ema2-dependent SUMOylation events might not be detected if Ema2-dependent and Ema2-independent SUMOylation occur in the same proteins
source: Although, we failed to detect any other protein that was SUMOylated in an Ema2-dependent manner (Figure 5A), some Ema2-dependent SUMOylation events might not be detected in our current approach if Ema2-dependent and Ema2-independent SUMOylation occur in the same proteins and/or if Ema2-dependent SUMOylation results in protein degradation, such as through SUMO-targeted ubiquitination (Praefcke et al., 2012; Staudinger, 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for the failure to detect other Ema2-dependent SUMOylation targets.

claim: Some Ema2-dependent SUMOylation events might not be detected if Ema2-dependent SUMOylation results in protein degradation
source: Although, we failed to detect any other protein that was SUMOylated in an Ema2-dependent manner (Figure 5A), some Ema2-dependent SUMOylation events might not be detected in our current approach if Ema2-dependent and Ema2-independent SUMOylation occur in the same proteins and/or if Ema2-dependent SUMOylation results in protein degradation, such as through SUMO-targeted ubiquitination (Praefcke et al., 2012; Staudinger, 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as a possible explanation for the failure to detect other Ema2-dependent SUMOylation targets.

claim: SUMOylation of Spt6 may promote pMAC-lncRNA transcription by competing with some other modification that occurs at the same lysine residue(s)
source: Alternatively, SUMOylation of Spt6 may promote pMAC-lncRNA transcription by competing with some other modification that occurs at the same lysine residue(s) and our SUMOylation-defective Spt6 mutant might actually mimic the SUMOylated state of Spt6 by preventing such modification.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposed as an alternative explanation for the observation that SUMOylation-defective Spt6 still supports lncRNA transcription.

claim: SUMOylation of the heterochromatin components Swi6, Chp2, and Clr4 is important for RNAi-directed heterochromatin silencing in fission yeast
source: It was reported that SUMOylation of the heterochromatin components Swi6, Chp2, and Clr4 is important for RNAi-directed heterochromatin silencing in fission yeast (Shin et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: SUMOylation of the histone deacetylase HDAC1 promotes small RNA-directed transcriptional silencing in C. elegans
source: Additionally, SUMOylation of the histone deacetylase HDAC1 promotes small RNA-directed transcriptional silencing in C. elegans (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The SUMO E3 ligase Su(var)2–10 plays an essential role in the recruitment of the histone methyltransferase complex SetDB1 in Drosophila piRNA-directed transposon silencing
source: Furthermore, in the piRNA-directed transposon silencing of Drosophila, the SUMO E3 ligase Su(var)2–10 plays an essential role in the recruitment of the histone methyltransferase complex SetDB1, which deposits H3K9me3 (Ninova et al., 2020a; Ninova et al., 2020b), and Su(var)2–10-independent SUMOylation of Panoramix (Panx) also promotes transcriptional silencing by recruiting the general heterochromatin effector Sov (Andreev et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Su(var)2–10-independent SUMOylation of Panoramix (Panx) promotes transcriptional silencing by recruiting the general heterochromatin effector Sov in Drosophila
source: Furthermore, in the piRNA-directed transposon silencing of Drosophila, the SUMO E3 ligase Su(var)2–10 plays an essential role in the recruitment of the histone methyltransferase complex SetDB1, which deposits H3K9me3 (Ninova et al., 2020a; Ninova et al., 2020b), and Su(var)2–10-independent SUMOylation of Panoramix (Panx) also promotes transcriptional silencing by recruiting the general heterochromatin effector Sov (Andreev et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: All SUMOylation events in fission yeast, C. elegans, and Drosophila seem to require pre-existing lncRNA transcription
source: All these SUMOylation events seem to require pre-existing lncRNA transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited studies about SUMOylation in other organisms.

claim: Ema2-dependent SUMOylation during the process of DNA elimination in Tetrahymena occurs upstream of lncRNA transcription
source: In contrast, this study showed that Ema2-dependent SUMOylation during the process of DNA elimination in Tetrahymena occurs upstream of lncRNA transcription (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the findings of this study.

claim: The loss of the Piwi protein Twi1 blocks the accumulation of H3K27me3 in the parental MAC without affecting lncRNA accumulation
source: In addition, the fact that the loss of the Piwi protein Twi1 blocks the accumulation of H3K27me3 in the parental MAC (Liu et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2021) without affecting lncRNA accumulation (Woo et al., 2016) indicates that heterochromatin formation is not a prerequisite for lncRNA transcription in Tetrahymena, in contrast to heterochromatin-dependent lncRNA transcription of piRNA clusters in Drosophila (Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Heterochromatin formation is not a prerequisite for lncRNA transcription in Tetrahymena
source: In addition, the fact that the loss of the Piwi protein Twi1 blocks the accumulation of H3K27me3 in the parental MAC (Liu et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2021) without affecting lncRNA accumulation (Woo et al., 2016) indicates that heterochromatin formation is not a prerequisite for lncRNA transcription in Tetrahymena, in contrast to heterochromatin-dependent lncRNA transcription of piRNA clusters in Drosophila (Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that lncRNA transcription occurs without heterochromatin formation in Tetrahymena.

claim: Tetrahymena likely uses a unique evolutionary solution for transcribing lncRNAs to promote TDSD and small RNA-directed heterochromatin formation
source: Altogether, Tetrahymena likely uses a unique evolutionary solution for transcribing lncRNAs to promote TDSD and small RNA-directed heterochromatin formation.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of Tetrahymena with other organisms.

claim: Further investigations of the role of Ema2-dependent SUMOylation in lncRNA transcription will clarify an undescribed layer of regulatory mechanisms in small RNA-directed chromatin regulation
source: We, therefore, believe that further investigations of the role of Ema2-dependent SUMOylation in lncRNA transcription will clarify an undescribed layer of regulatory mechanisms in small RNA-directed chromatin regulation.
evidence: The claim is speculative, representing the authors' perspective on future research directions.
